Really solid, interesting gameplay mechanics and plot premise completely and utterly ruined by subpar writing creeping throughout the entire game from start to finish. Twists are entirely predictable, some (not all) characters react unnaturally to events, "intelligent" characters completely act against their own interests, game acts like you should care about characters you have absolutely 0 bond with, very rushed last chapter which does not work because of the aforementioned missing character depth. 

I assume LOTS of players will strongly dislike the last 5 minutes of gameplay, and though I like the general idea and premise of it, I think it's execution was badly done and almost insults the player for having used their time playing this game.

TL;DR really really strong mechanical and conceptual bones, terrible terrible writing

Solid thriller/investigation game; I really enjoyed my time with it. The dialogue feels uncommonly natural and well-written, and the voice acting is strong as well. Creatively speaking, it's got some fresh style choices too: I really liked how they did the "cutscenes" in particular.

I'm sure some would complain about the short length and the fact that you choices don't change the path of the story, but for me those things don't count for much.

Overall, I'm impressed, and I think this game has the unique qualities and strong execution needed to stand out in the crowd.

Plot is pretty interesting and the gameplay is pretty fun. Unfortunately all the cases are exclusively focused on the main plot. It would have been interesting to have things a little more spread out and do either some generic cases or a much beefier plot because it feels like you're aggressively pushed into making bigger plot connections rather than uncovering them on your own. Usually filler is a negative but this game would absolutely have benefited from it. Similarly so for the freedom to explore more connections yourself.

It also struggles a little because you're given a few different tools but they're largely only used for one or two cases. Specifically the chemical analysis capability or bomb defusal but the vehicle one too. It would have been nice to have those elements used more and if there were some filler cases, it would have felt less forced.

It's a unique experience and fun to play. The concept works and I think it could be refined in subsequent games if the developer was so inclined.

Still playing and loving it. I hope the developer has Operator 2 in the development. As long as it stays like this, I would buy the next one. I was looking for something close to Cyber Manhunt Series and this fits the bill IMHO.

I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.

This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

Amazing production value on this game. All my issues that I had upon reflection were basically nonexistent at the time of playing, and only upon reaching the end of the game did they solidify in my mind.

Namely, that most of the puzzling aspects of the game are more guided setpieces. 
The potential of things like the terminal, the GUI, etc, are limited to exactly one interaction.
The ending is a big open wound and comes very abruptly -- just as, in my eyes, the story was just starting to ramp up.
And said ending essentially undoes most of what you did in the game, narratively.
Your ability to interact with the game UI is usually heavily restricted unlike other "hacker" type games that use this presentation style.
In short, everything but the presentation quality is a bit undercooked. Get it on sale, if anything.

Outside of one really great and tense sequence it's mostly clicking through simple instructions and doing some deductions to progress. It's interesting and compelling but the playtime is lacking to fully explore the concept. The store description mentions working on many cases and assisting agents but everything done is very attached to the central story where some more diversity in content of the cases would be appreciated to pad out the fantasy of doing the detective work and better utilize the mechanics introduced. I wish it was easier to play though certain sections of the game to make different choices without playing through the whole game again.

I would recommend this game on sale but at full price, it's too quick to finish to enjoy completely.

As an avid fan of narrative-driven puzzle games, I recently delved into "The Operator," developed by Bureau 81. Released on July 22, 2024, this game offers a unique experience by placing players in the role of Evan Tanner, an operator at the fictional Federal Defence Intelligence agency. Your primary task is to assist field agents by analysing evidence and providing real-time support, all from behind a computer screen.

The game's immersive design truly makes you feel like a part of a larger investigative team. The puzzles are well-crafted, requiring keen attention to detail without becoming overly frustrating. Each case you handle reveals a piece of a larger conspiracy, keeping your curiosity piqued from start to finish. The narrative is compelling, reminiscent of classic detective stories, and unfolds at a pace that keeps you engaged throughout the approximately five-hour gameplay. 


However, the game isn't without its flaws. Some plot twists are predictable, and the voice acting can be hit-or-miss at times. Additionally, while the main storyline is captivating, I found myself wishing for more side cases to further explore the game's mechanics and world. 


In conclusion, "The Operator" is a commendable addition to the narrative puzzle genre. It offers an immersive and engaging experience that is well worth your time, especially if you're a fan of detective stories and investigative gameplay. Despite its minor shortcomings, it stands out as a solid and enjoyable game.

The game really was not what I expected. From the store page, I thought it would be fairly puzzle focused, with a lot of scanning evidence and connecting dots. But in reality, it plays out more like a visual novel with some very simple puzzles thrown in. There were multiple elements that seemed like they would be recurring features, but were used a single time and never again. Many pieces of evidence are teased, but are never actually shown before the game ends. The game feels like it ends *way* too quickly. It took me just over three hours to finish. I'm fine with shorter games, but there's so much potential here that goes nowhere because the game ends so soon.

On the plus side, the presentation is great. Despite mostly being a computer screen, the visuals have a certain flare to them that leans into the setting. The soundtrack compliments the narrative at every step, swelling at big reveals and calming down after tense moments. And the voice actors give solid performances. No complaints on this aspect.

As for the narrative, it's fairly compelling. You can definitely see a lot of the twists coming before they happen, but the presentation makes it interesting to see play out regardless. That being said, it again suffers from being too short. You're meant to be unraveling a big conspiracy over the course of the game, but by the time it's over, it feels like you've barely stuck your toes in. I was invested in what was happening, had just had a big reveal, and then... suddenly the credits are rolling.

There are definitely things to like about this game, but I have a hard time recommending it, especially if your mostly here for that "Investigation" tag. It's too short, too easy, and doesn't quite live up to what it says on the box. It feels like a demo for a larger game, but I kind of just wanted the larger game to begin with.

I have to gently recommend it. The voice acting was an especial highlight for me, the characters were fleshed out, and the puzzles themselves were clever and satisfying and never repetitive. 

It's when the game steps outside its puzzles that it struggles; For example, all of the cutscenes are filmed as if through someone's closed eyelids, which just didn't work for me - I didn't enjoy only knowing a blurry light on the screen was a fridge by the sound cues, especially when the character themselves sees fine. Long, unskippable audiobooks of the character's routine before and after work.

I'd suggest you just treat this as a puzzle game and not as a story game, despite how much emphasis the game puts on its narrative. It becomes pretty clear that the puzzle design is where the passion of this game lies, and the writing was only really added at the end of the process to string things together. If you know that in advance, though, you'll enjoy the experience a lot more.
